title: Sound Becomes a Signal
outcome: By the end, I can connect ordered sound samples to timing and explain what a maximum loses.
scenario: A fictional microphone display records five samples during a short classroom tap.
given: Signal A: 0,3,0,1,0. Signal B: 0,1,0,3,0. Toy values are signed measurement units; these happen to be nonnegative.

steps.label: Timed sampling
steps.detail: Associate every measurement with its sampling time.

steps.label: Signal A
steps.detail: Its largest sample 3 occurs at 1 ms.

steps.label: Signal B
steps.detail: Its largest sample 3 occurs at 3 ms.

steps.label: Maximum summary
steps.detail: Both maxima are 3, but the strongest recorded tap arrives at different times.

explanation: The sequences contain the same values in different orders. Keeping the maximum preserves peak recorded value while losing its timing. A graph should keep time on the horizontal axis; shuffling samples changes the recorded signal even if its maximum stays fixed.

counterfactual.reason: The selected times omit both nonzero samples from each signal.

student_task: Does the all-zero retained record prove the full signal was silent? Use the picture.
teacher_answer: No. The full supplied signals contain nonzero values at 1 and 3 ms; those measurements were discarded.
project_evidence: Record the sorter’s sampling interval and retain relevant sequences when a decision depends on changes over time.
limits: These sparse toy values cannot establish perceived loudness, pitch or what happened between sampling times.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
